related_questions.question: How long do you have to pay off a reverse mortgage after death?

text_blocks.snippet: After the death of a reverse mortgage borrower, heirs generally have 30 days to decide whether to keep the home, sell it, or turn it over to the lender. Extensions, typically up to six months, are often granted to allow heirs time to sell or refinance. If the loan balance is higher than the home's value, heirs may only need to pay 95% of the appraised value.

list.title: The Loan Becomes Due:
list.snippet: The reverse mortgage loan becomes due and payable upon the death of the borrower (and any co-borrowers or eligible non-borrowing spouses).

list.title: 30-Day Notification Period:
list.snippet: The lender must formally notify the heirs that the loan is due, and heirs have 30 days to decide on a course of action.
Keep the Home: Heirs can pay off the loan balance, potentially through refinancing, or pay 95% of the home's appraised value if it's lower than the loan balance.
Sell the Home: Heirs can sell the property to satisfy the loan and keep any remaining equity.
Turn Over the Home: Heirs can deed the property back to the lender to satisfy the debt.

list.title: Potential Extensions:
list.snippet: Lenders often grant extensions, usually up to six months, to allow heirs time to sell the home or secure financing to pay off the loan. In some cases, two 90-day extensions may be granted, providing up to 12 months to settle the loan if the home is being sold.
Non-Borrowing Spouse: If there is a non-borrowing spouse, they may have additional rights and options, such as being able to remain in the home under certain conditions.
Estate Planning: It's wise for homeowners with reverse mortgages to create an estate plan to help their heirs understand their options and navigate the process.
Communication with Lender: Open communication with the lender is crucial throughout the process to ensure a smooth transition.

related_questions.question: Can you negotiate a reverse mortgage payoff?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, in some cases, it is possible to negotiate a reverse mortgage payoff, particularly if the loan balance exceeds the home's current market value. Lenders may be willing to negotiate, especially if the borrower is facing financial hardship or if the loan is underwater.
Here's a breakdown of how negotiation works and what factors are involved:

list.title: When can you negotiate?
list.snippet: Reverse mortgages become due and payable when the borrower dies, sells the home, or permanently moves out. You can also negotiate if you're experiencing financial hardship.

list.title: Why negotiate?
list.snippet: If the home's value is less than the loan balance (underwater), negotiating can help reduce the payoff amount.

list.title: What factors do lenders consider?
list.snippet: Lenders assess the current market value, the outstanding loan balance, the borrower's financial situation, the property's condition, and any other debts on the property.
Review your agreement: Carefully examine your reverse mortgage contract to understand the terms, including any penalties for early payoff.
Contact your lender: Discuss your situation and your willingness to negotiate with your lender.
Prepare documentation: Gather financial information like income statements and tax returns to support your case.
Consider professional help: Consulting with a financial advisor or attorney can be beneficial during the negotiation process.

list.title: Alternatives to negotiation:
list.snippet: If negotiation isn't successful, you can explore other options like refinancing with a traditional mortgage or selling the home to pay off the reverse mortgage.
HUD (the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development) backs most reverse mortgages, and they will cover the difference if the home is underwater and the loan is assigned to them.
If you are the heir to a property with a reverse mortgage, you can pay off the loan at the current balance or 95% of the home's current value, whichever is less.
You can also negotiate a deed-in-lieu of foreclosure, which means transferring the home's title to the lender to satisfy the debt.
